properties.name: EVERY change to the implemented design carries a test, and regression cover — not only an identified issue, and not only the change's own happy path
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-09-22: *"with each change to the implemented design, we need to have clear testing (and regression testing to ensure we don't go backwards or that the change doesn't break something else)."*

TWO HALVES, and the second is the one usually missing:
① THE CHANGE HAS A TEST that says what it now does.
② THE CHANGE HAS REGRESSION COVER — evidence it did not undo something that already worked, and did not break something adjacent. "We don't go backwards" is his phrase, and it is the half a passing new test says nothing about.

═══ POWER: GATE-BLOCKING, ON HIS WORD, TWICE ═══

`enforced: true`. Asked what should happen when somebody lands a change to a built capability with no test behind it — good change, everything else green — he chose STOP THE BUILD (2026-09-22). Put to him again after the measurement below, with the cliff it implies, he held: *"we can revisit 'stop the build' if that is wrong."* So it is his word, taken knowingly, and explicitly revisable rather than final.

═══ WHY THIS IS NOT `rule:an-issue-is-root-caused-then-pinned-by-a-test-then-fixed`, WHICH WAS READ BEFORE WRITING THIS ═══

That rule (2026-08-26) covers an IDENTIFIED ISSUE and prescribes the ORDER — root-cause, pin with a failing test, fix, test, write the cause down. This one is WIDER in scope and different in power: it binds EVERY change, including a new feature nobody reported a defect against, and it is gate-blocking where that one is advisory. The order rule still governs when the change is a repair; this one says a change needs cover whatever prompted it.

⚠️ THEY DISAGREE ON POWER, AND THIS NODE DOES NOT SETTLE THAT. A change that repairs an issue falls under both. Whether the older rule should now be revised upward is HIS — recording a broader enforced rule does not silently re-settle a narrower advisory one.

AND IT IS NOT `dec:idea-how-does-a-testing-standard-arrive-without-a-day-one-cliff`, also read: that is the DELIVERY question — how a standard like this arrives without failing the build over history. This is the standard itself. One is what must be true; the other is how it is introduced, and collapsing them is how a correct rule gets switched off in its first week.

═══ 🛑 WHAT ENFORCEMENT CAN AND CANNOT SEE — READ BEFORE BUILDING THE DETECTOR ═══

The 2026-08-26 rule records, from the same owner, exactly why ITS enforcement was declined, and that reasoning is not retracted here — it is inherited as a constraint on how THIS rule is checked:

  "nothing in a diff or a CI run can see whether a test was FAILING before the fix — CI only ever
   runs the merged state. So an enforced version could only check something weaker — does this
   change touch code and add no test? — which passes on a test written AFTER the fix. A check that
   reads as enforcement while measuring something else is worse than no check, because it converts
   an unanswered question into a false green."

⇒ THE DETECTOR THIS RULE OWES MUST STATE WHAT IT MEASURES. It can honestly check that a change touching a realized capability arrives with a check attached, and that the check RAN. It cannot check that the check was red first, and it must not imply that it did.

═══ ⚠️ THE GROUND IT LANDS ON, MEASURED 2026-09-22 ═══

    312 Verifications, 311 reading `passing`, 282 WITH NO EXECUTABLE FORM, 46 never run
    47 of 288 capabilities have no passing check
    448 of 598 artifacts never confirmed against what they realize
    line/branch coverage of 88,815 lines: never measured

Enforcing this against existing ground fails the build on day one, and a gate that does that is a gate somebody switches off — this project has said so in its own words and grandfathered twice for exactly that reason. Recording the rule as enforced states the STANDARD; it does not authorise a detector that goes red over history.

═══ WHAT IT OWES, PLAINLY ═══

An `enforced: true` rule owes a detector: `unverified_enforced_rule` (0.6) asks what checks it and keeps asking until a PASSING Verification is attached — a `planned` check does not silence it. And per this design's standing warning: never attach a check in order to close the finding. Attach it because it detects the violation; if it does not, leave the finding open and say so.
